A vocabulary for careful thinking.

134 terms to revisit. Use these as entry points, not definitions detached from their methods. The chapter links restore context.

Abduction
Developing a plausible explanation for observations. It generates candidates that still need comparison with alternatives, not automatic proof of the best-sounding story.
Read in context
Abstract
A compressed account of a work's question, approach, contribution and limits. It is a discovery aid, not a substitute for inspecting the supporting argument or methods.
Read in context
Accuracy
Closeness to an appropriate target or reference value. A procedure can be highly repeatable yet consistently wrong.
Read in context
Alternative hypothesis
A competing statistical hypothesis defined for a test. Rejecting the null does not establish every substantive explanation compatible with the alternative.
Read in context
Analysis plan
A record of how data or material will be processed and interpreted, including important comparisons, exclusions and uncertainty. Changes should remain visible.
Read in context
Anonymization
Reducing identifying information so individuals cannot reasonably be identified under relevant conditions; context and linkage risks matter. It is stronger than merely removing names.
Read in context
Artifact
An inspectable output or object used in research: code, data, a model, instrument, prototype, protocol or document. Its existence is not evidence that its main claim is valid.
Read in context
Assumption
A premise on which an inference or method depends. Some are mathematical stipulations; others are substantive claims that need evidence or sensitivity analysis.
Read in context
Audit trail
A record of decisions, transformations and interpretations that helps another person reconstruct how the work developed.
Read in context
Authorship
A responsibility and credit relationship governed by relevant disciplinary, venue and institutional criteria. Contributor roles and acknowledgments are related but not identical.
Read in context
Baseline
A justified reference condition or prior method against which an approach is compared. A deliberately weak baseline can inflate apparent improvement.
Read in context
Bayes factor
A comparison of marginal likelihoods under specified competing models. Its interpretation depends on the models and priors; it is not directly the posterior probability of a hypothesis.
Read in context
Bayesian updating
Combining a prior distribution with the likelihood of observed data to obtain a posterior distribution, conditional on the model.
Read in context
Bias
Systematic distortion relative to a target inference or measurement. More observations can reduce sampling noise while leaving the bias intact.
Read in context
Blinding
Limiting knowledge of assignments or expected outcomes where appropriate to reduce particular influences on behavior or assessment. It does not eliminate every bias.
Read in context
Case study
An in-depth investigation of a bounded case or cases. Its inferential value depends on case selection, context, evidence and analytic logic, not just small sample size.
Read in context
Causal effect
A contrast between outcomes under specified interventions or conditions. The intervention, comparison, population and timescale must be clear.
Read in context
Causal identification
Establishing how a causal target can be recovered from available information under explicit assumptions. It is distinct from numerical estimation.
Read in context
Citation
An attribution and locator connecting a statement to a source. It does not guarantee that the source exists as described, supports the wording, or is correct.
Read in context
Citation chasing
Following references backward or later citing works forward. It expands discovery but can amplify the visibility of already well-connected literature.
Read in context
Claim
A statement that can carry a support obligation. Its meaning includes qualifiers, domain, assumptions and intended strength.
Read in context
Claim ledger
A structured map of consequential statements to their sources, assumptions, checks, objections and current support. It improves traceability, not truth by itself.
Read in context
Coding
Applying analytic labels to qualitative material or other observations according to an explicit approach. A code is not automatically a theme or explanation.
Read in context
Collider
A variable represented as a common effect of other variables in a causal model. Conditioning on it can create an association and bias an inference.
Read in context
Comprehensive
Covering important relevant dimensions within a stated scope. It does not establish that literally every relevant source has been found.
Read in context
Conceptual framework
An organized set of concepts and proposed relationships that guides inquiry. It should clarify questions and assumptions rather than rename them impressively.
Read in context
Confidence interval
An interval produced by a procedure with a specified long-run coverage property under assumptions. It is not ordinarily a posterior probability statement about a fixed parameter.
Read in context
Confirmatory analysis
Testing specified expectations with analysis decisions set independently of the evidence used for that test, while making deviations and assumptions transparent.
Read in context
Confounder
A variable or factor that offers a competing explanation for an exposure–outcome association, often represented as a cause of both in a causal model.
Read in context
Construct
A concept of interest, such as trust or learning, that requires a justified relationship to the observations or arguments used to study it.
Read in context
Construct validity
The adequacy of interpreting an operation or measure as capturing the intended construct. A convenient proxy may not support a broad conceptual claim.
Read in context
Contribution
What completed research adds to knowledge or practice. It is not simply the activity performed, the software built, or the novelty promised.
Read in context
Controlled vocabulary
A standardized set of indexing terms used by a database or field. It can complement free-text synonyms; exact syntax and indexing vary by platform.
Read in context
Counterexample
A case that violates a statement's claimed conditions and conclusion, thereby refuting that statement in its stated form. A case outside its assumptions is not a counterexample.
Read in context
Counterfactual
An outcome or state considered under an alternative condition or intervention. Answering such a question requires a model and assumptions, not only observed association.
Read in context
Credible interval
A Bayesian interval summarizing posterior probability under a specified model, data and prior. It should not be silently interchanged with a confidence interval.
Read in context
CRediT
A taxonomy of contributor roles that helps describe who did what in a research output. It does not replace the relevant authorship policy.
Read in context
Critical appraisal
Examining a source's design, conduct, analysis, reporting and applicability for the inference you want to use. It is not a prestige score.
Read in context
Data dictionary
Documentation of variables, units, permissible values, coding and meaning. It helps prevent datasets from becoming uninterpretable collections of columns.
Read in context
Data leakage
Information entering model development or evaluation that would not be available at the intended decision point, or that compromises a supposed holdout boundary.
Read in context
Deduction
Deriving a conclusion that follows logically from premises. A valid inference does not, on its own, establish that the premises are true or applicable.
Read in context
Deduplication
Identifying repeated records or representations. Removing duplicate citations does not automatically remove multiple reports of the same study or dataset.
Read in context
Definition
A stipulation or clarification of meaning used in an argument. Useful definitions must remain consistent, and empirical adequacy is a separate question.
Read in context
Dependent evidence
Evidence sharing participants, data, assumptions, procedures or other influences. Treating it as independent corroboration can exaggerate confidence.
Read in context
Dissemination
Communicating research through papers, repositories, talks or other forms. The reach of communication is distinct from the strength of the underlying evidence.
Read in context
DOI
A persistent identifier used to locate an object such as a publication or dataset. It identifies an object; it does not certify quality, truth or peer-review status.
Read in context
Effect size
A measure of the magnitude of a contrast or relationship on a specified scale. Importance depends on context, uncertainty and the consequences of the effect.
Read in context
Eligibility criteria
Rules determining which sources, studies, cases or participants belong in a specified inquiry. They should not be adjusted invisibly to favor a result.
Read in context
Empirical
Grounded in observations or experience collected and interpreted through a method. Empirical evidence still depends on measurement and inference choices.
Read in context
Epistemology
The study or working account of knowledge and justification: what counts as knowing, and what warrants a claim.
Read in context
Equivalence test
An analysis designed to assess whether a difference is small enough relative to prespecified meaningful bounds. It is not simply a non-significant ordinary test.
Read in context
Estimand
The precise quantity or contrast the inquiry aims to estimate, including the relevant population, conditions and outcome definition.
Read in context
Estimation
Using observations and a method to obtain a numerical estimate of a target. A precise estimate does not fix an unidentified or poorly defined target.
Read in context
Ethics review
Assessment under applicable institutional and regulatory requirements for research conduct, especially where people, animals or sensitive information are involved.
Read in context
Evidence
Information or argument that bears on a particular claim through a justified connection. A source can be relevant without decisively supporting the conclusion.
Read in context
Exclusion reason
A recorded explanation for why a candidate source or case did not meet eligibility criteria. Lack of access must not masquerade as an assessed methodological exclusion.
Read in context
Exhaustive
An ambition to find all relevant material within a specified search universe. It is a bounded coverage claim, not a promise of omniscience.
Read in context
Exclusive
Restricted to some people or things, or excluding others. It does not mean exhaustive.
Read in context
Exploratory analysis
Investigating patterns, developing questions or generating hypotheses. Valuable discovery work should not be disguised afterward as a prespecified confirmatory test.
Read in context
External validity
The justification for extending an inference beyond the studied setting, population or conditions. A result's local credibility does not establish broad applicability.
Read in context
FAIR
Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable principles for digital research resources. Appropriate access restrictions can coexist with FAIR practice.
Read in context
Falsification
Subjecting a claim to evidence or argument that could contradict it. A failed auxiliary assumption or measurement complicates what exactly an empirical test has refuted.
Read in context
Formal verification
Checking specified formal properties relative to a formal system and trusted process. The match to an informal requirement remains a separate obligation.
Read in context
Generalization
Extending a conclusion beyond the observed cases. Its warrant depends on design, assumptions, context and the kind of inference, not only sample size.
Read in context
Grey literature
Relevant material outside conventional commercial academic publishing, such as reports or theses. Discovery and quality assessment may require different strategies.
Read in context
HARKing
Presenting a hypothesis developed after seeing results as though it had been specified beforehand. Transparent exploratory reporting avoids that misrepresentation.
Read in context
Heterogeneity
Variation among studies, effects or contexts. Its source may be substantive, methodological or statistical; a single statistic does not fully explain it.
Read in context
Hypothesis
A candidate answer or expectation that can be investigated or criticized. It should not be treated as established merely because it is plausible.
Read in context
IMRaD
Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion: a common empirical paper structure, not a universal requirement for every research genre.
Read in context
Independence
A property of observations, sources or reviews relevant to inference. Distinct-looking records or multiple agents can still share important dependencies.
Read in context
Induction
Reasoning beyond observed cases toward a more general claim. The extension needs a justification tied to sampling, context or the structure of the phenomenon.
Read in context
Inference
The reasoning that connects evidence or premises to a conclusion. Different kinds of inference require different assumptions and checks.
Read in context
Informed consent
A context-sensitive process supporting voluntary participation with adequate understanding, rather than merely obtaining a signature.
Read in context
Internal validity
The credibility of an inference within a study; often used for whether an observed contrast supports the intended causal interpretation.
Read in context
Intervention
A specified change or assignment whose consequences are of interest. It must be defined precisely enough to distinguish it from merely observing an exposure.
Read in context
Literature review
An examination and synthesis of relevant scholarly work. Its type, scope, search method and appraisal obligations should be stated.
Read in context
Mechanism
An account of how a phenomenon or artifact produces an outcome. A descriptive correlation, label or flowchart does not automatically establish one.
Read in context
Mediator
A variable represented along a proposed causal pathway between an exposure/intervention and an outcome. Its role depends on the causal model and question.
Read in context
Meta-analysis
A statistical synthesis of appropriately comparable estimates. Pooling does not remove bias, incompatibility or dependence among the inputs.
Read in context
Metadata
Information describing a source or object, such as title, authors, version or identifier. Resolving metadata is not the same as reading or validating the object.
Read in context
Method
A procedure used to investigate, collect, analyze, interpret, construct or prove something.
Read in context
Methodology
The rationale and logic that justify how a set of methods can answer a question. It is more than a list of tools.
Read in context
Mixed methods
Intentional integration of quantitative and qualitative components to address a research question. Parallel disconnected analyses do not automatically achieve integration.
Read in context
Model
A selective representation of something for a purpose. Its usefulness and limits depend on which distinctions it preserves and which it leaves out.
Read in context
Novelty
A defensible difference from relevant existing work. New to the author is not necessarily new to the field, and novelty alone does not establish importance.
Read in context
Null hypothesis
A specified statistical hypothesis used as a reference in a test. Its rejection does not automatically prove a favored mechanism.
Read in context
Ontology
An account of what kinds of things exist or are treated as real in an inquiry. Ontological choices can affect what is measured and explained.
Read in context
Operationalization
Specifying how a concept will be observed, measured or otherwise represented in an investigation.
Read in context
P-value
A probability of a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one under a specified null model and test rule. It is not the probability that the null is true.
Read in context
Parameter
A quantity in a model or population that is treated as unknown and may be estimated. Its meaning depends on the model and target.
Read in context
Peer review
Critical assessment by relevant reviewers under a venue's process. It is scrutiny, not a guarantee of validity or universal consensus.
Read in context
Pilot study
Preliminary work that assesses feasibility or refines procedures. Its purpose, changes and relationship to later confirmatory work should be explicit.
Read in context
Population
The set of units about which a question is asked. The accessible sample may differ from this target in consequential ways.
Read in context
Positivity / overlap
A causal-inference requirement that relevant treatment/comparison possibilities occur for the covariate patterns needed for the target effect, under the chosen design.
Read in context
Power
The probability a test rejects the null under a specified alternative and design. It is not a fixed property of a sample size alone.
Read in context
Precision
How tightly an estimate is determined under a procedure. High precision does not guarantee low bias or valid interpretation.
Read in context
Prediction interval
An interval for future observations under a model, distinct from an interval for an unknown mean or other parameter.
Read in context
Preregistration
A time-stamped record of a research/analysis plan made before the relevant confirmatory test. Deviations and exploratory work remain possible when transparently reported.
Read in context
Preprint
A publicly shared manuscript version that may precede or lack formal peer review. Cite its exact version and do not infer journal acceptance.
Read in context
Prior art
Existing relevant ideas, methods, systems or disclosures against which a proposed contribution is compared. Legal patent usage has additional specific rules.
Read in context
Proof obligation
A statement or step that must be established for a dependent argument to hold. A missing necessary obligation blocks unconditional completion.
Read in context
Protocol
A specified plan for how an inquiry or procedure will be conducted, including relevant decisions, responsibilities and boundaries.
Read in context
Provenance
The origin and transformation history of an object or claim, including versions, sources and responsible actions.
Read in context
Pseudonymization
Replacing identifiers while potentially retaining a way to reconnect records to people. It is not a guarantee of anonymity.
Read in context
Publication bias
Distortion arising when whether or how work becomes available depends on its results or perceived interest.
Read in context
Purposive sampling
Selecting cases for their relevance to an inquiry's aims. It is not automatically a probability sample for estimating population prevalence.
Read in context
Qualitative research
Inquiry into meaning, experience, practice, process or context through appropriate interpretive methodologies. It is not simply small-sample statistics.
Read in context
Random assignment
Allocating units to conditions by a chance mechanism. It is distinct from randomly sampling a population and does not solve every validity problem.
Read in context
Reflexivity
Examining how the researcher's position, decisions and relationships shape an inquiry. It supports accountability rather than making interpretation disappear.
Read in context
Registered report
A publication format that typically reviews the question and proposed methods before results are known. Exact commitments and acceptance conditions depend on the venue.
Read in context
Reliability
Consistency of a measure or procedure under specified conditions. It does not by itself show that the intended construct was captured.
Read in context
Replication
A term for repeating or independently testing results whose operational definition varies by community. State what was repeated, by whom, with which data/artifacts.
Read in context
Reproducibility
The ability to obtain or examine results again under declared conditions; terminology varies. Specify whether this means rerunning code, repeating procedures or obtaining new evidence.
Read in context
Research gap
A consequential absence, unresolved issue or inadequacy in existing knowledge or practice. Merely unstudied is not automatically important.
Read in context
Retraction
A formal withdrawal or major warning about a publication. Preserve its status and reconsider dependent affirmative claims; the source can still be studied as an object.
Read in context
Risk of bias
The risk of systematic error in a result or inference because of design, conduct, analysis or reporting. It is not identical to poor prose or lack of prestige.
Read in context
Robustness
How a conclusion behaves under relevant alternative assumptions, specifications or conditions. Passing a few convenient variations is not universal robustness.
Read in context
Sample
The units actually included or observed. Size alone does not establish representativeness, independence or adequacy for the question.
Read in context
Saturation
A family of qualitative sufficiency concepts with different meanings across approaches. Explain what has become sufficient and why that criterion fits.
Read in context
Scoping review
A review that maps concepts, evidence types or the extent of a literature using an explicit approach. It need not estimate one pooled effect.
Read in context
Sensitivity analysis
Examining how results change under plausible alternative assumptions, choices or values. It reveals dependence; it does not prove the chosen assumption true.
Read in context
Standard deviation
A measure of spread among observations. It is not the same as the standard error of an estimated quantity.
Read in context
Standard error
A measure of an estimator's variability under a model/design. It describes estimation uncertainty, not all possible sources of error.
Read in context
Statistical significance
A relation between a test result and a chosen decision threshold. It does not establish effect importance, causality or practical usefulness.
Read in context
Synthesis
An accountable account of relationships across evidence or arguments: convergence, contrast, explanation, boundary or unresolved conflict—not merely a sequence of summaries.
Read in context
Systematic review
A review addressing a defined question with explicit, organized methods for eligibility, search, selection, appraisal and synthesis.
Read in context
Theory
An explanatory/conceptual system whose meaning varies by discipline. Distinguish empirical explanation, mathematical theory, model, framework and conjecture.
Read in context
Transferability
Reasoned applicability of insights to other contexts, often emphasized in qualitative inquiry. Rich context helps readers judge it; it is not automatic universality.
Read in context
Triangulation
Using multiple perspectives, methods, sources or investigators to examine a question. Disagreement can be informative; convergence does not guarantee independent confirmation.
Read in context
Uncertainty
Limits on what is known or how precisely it is known. Sampling variability, measurement error, model uncertainty and missing knowledge require different treatments.
Read in context
Unit of analysis
The entity about which the analysis makes an inference. It may differ from the unit that produced each recorded observation.
Read in context
Validity
The defensibility of an interpretation or inference for its intended use. Different forms of validity address different threats.
Read in context
Verification
Checking specified properties against a defined standard or requirement. The result is limited to the version, procedure and scope actually checked.
Read in context
Warrant
The justified connection that allows evidence or premises to support a conclusion. Making it explicit is central to an inspectable argument.
Read in context

Sources, scope, and where to go deeper.

This handbook is an original educational synthesis built with focused Firecrawl searches and selected primary-page reads. It is not an exhaustive literature review. General explanations, glossary definitions and synthetic examples are authored teaching material; linked sources support specific distinctions, not every sentence or a universal method.

Source checks: 8 October 2026. Some responses were cached. Coverage below distinguishes full page text, selected passages, metadata and partial PDF reading. Automated extraction was not treated as infallible: overbroad PRISMA, FAIR-access and experiment-only causal phrasing was rejected or checked against the underlying text/specialist source.

The original learning text is retained. This edition uses Chief’s selected Forgis capture for visual direction; the capture’s tokens, section screenshots and hover evidence were inspected locally. Origin scripts, foundry media, logos and commercial claims are excluded. The original edition’s public editorial guidance from Tubik was text-only; no Details MCP retrieval is claimed.

  1. S01 / Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

    Scientific Method

    Philosophical orientation: methodology is contested and plural; no single recipe is imposed across every discipline.

    Reading scope: Firecrawl targeted answer; not the full entry. No extracted quotation is reproduced as a verified literal quote.

  2. S02 / PRISMA

    PRISMA 2020

    Reporting guideline, checklists and flow diagrams for systematic reviews. Reporting is distinct from conduct and validity.

    Reading scope: Official overview page text read. Linked statement and elaboration papers were not read in full for this guide.

  3. S03 / PRISMA

    PRISMA extension for scoping reviews

    Scoping reviews map evidence/concepts and use a distinct reporting extension, PRISMA-ScR.

    Reading scope: Official extension page text read; checklist PDFs and linked papers not read in full.

  4. S04 / Cochrane Handbook

    Chapter 4: Searching for and selecting studies

    Search coverage, sources, documentation and selection. This is intervention-review guidance; not a universal method for every field.

    Reading scope: Search excerpts and focused Firecrawl extraction; not the entire handbook.

  5. S05 / Center for Open Science

    Preregistration

    Distinguish planned confirmatory analyses from valuable exploratory work; report deviations transparently.

    Reading scope: Selected FAQ passages/search excerpts and targeted extraction, not every linked study.

  6. S06 / American Statistical Association · 2016

    ASA statement on statistical significance and p-values — release notice

    Six principles: p-values are not posterior hypothesis probabilities, effect size, practical importance or substitutes for reasoning.

    Reading scope: All three pages of the official notice extracted/read. The separate journal statement and commentaries were not all read.

  7. S07 / NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook

    Confidence limits for the mean

    Frequentist confidence intervals and their long-run interpretation under assumptions.

    Reading scope: Page text read. Extracted mathematical layout was imperfect; the guide does not copy its mangled equations.

  8. S08 / EQUATOR Network

    Standards for reporting qualitative research (SRQR)

    Locate appropriate qualitative reporting guidance; reporting standards are not a universal epistemology or proof of quality.

    Reading scope: Registry page read; not a claim of full reading of O’Brien et al.’s underlying paper.

  9. S09 / U.S. HHS / OHRP

    The Belmont Report

    Respect for persons, beneficence and justice in human-subject research. Local institutional/jurisdictional rules still apply.

    Reading scope: Selected principles and applications through Firecrawl extraction/search passages; not a legal or ethics-approval determination.

  10. S10 / GO FAIR Foundation

    The FAIR Guiding Principles

    Findability, accessibility, interoperability, reuse, provenance and licenses; authorization may be needed, not universally required.

    Reading scope: Full principles page text read after checking an overbroad generated extraction.

  11. S11 / ACM

    Artifact Review and Badging v1.1

    Separate artifact availability/evaluation from results validation; define reproduction/replication in the policy’s own terms.

    Reading scope: Policy text was read earlier in this conversation; version rechecked through Firecrawl here. No badge is awarded by this handbook.

  12. S12 / Lean Language Reference

    Validating a Lean Proof

    Trusted targets, statement correspondence, transitive axioms, incomplete proofs and checker trust boundaries.

    Reading scope: Relevant official sections read earlier in this conversation and targeted extraction revisited here. No proof tool was executed.

  13. S13 / NISO / CRediT

    Contributor Role Taxonomy

    Fourteen contributor roles make different contributions visible; use the relevant separate authorship policy.

    Reading scope: Official resource hub page read. Linked role pages and every venue’s authorship policy were not individually reviewed.

  14. S14 / OpenStax · Psychology 2e

    Approaches to Research

    Introductory orientation to study approaches, surveys, cases and longitudinal/cross-sectional designs.

    Reading scope: Focused Firecrawl extraction only; not the full book. Introductory generalizations are not treated as universal guarantees.

  15. S15 / OpenStax · Psychology 2e

    Analyzing Findings

    Introductory distinctions among association, assignment, measurement reliability and validity.

    Reading scope: Focused extraction. Its overbroad experiment-only causal phrasing was not adopted; see the specialist causal source S16.

  16. S16 / Judea Pearl · Statistics Surveys 3 (2009), 96–146

    Causal inference in statistics: An overview

    Causal/counterfactual inference combines data with explicit assumptions; identification and estimation are distinct operations.

    Reading scope: First three PDF pages only: abstract, contents and introduction (printed pp. 96–98), not all 51 pages. DOI 10.1214/09-SS057 confirmed in the source.

The aim is not to sound certain.
It is to know what your answer can bear.
